assessment.nobel_worthiness: A theoretical prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle, followed by the experimental discovery of correlated-insulator and superconducting states, opened an entirely new tunable platform for strongly correlated physics. The discovery is clear, original and has spawned a large, independently reproduced field.
assessment.attribution: The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model supplied the prediction and the Jarillo-Herrero group the decisive experimental discovery; this pairing of theory and experiment gives a natural three-person configuration. Other experimental groups made major contributions that this credit list does not capture.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many independent groups within about eight years; the phenomenology is stable even though the microscopic mechanism of superconductivity is still debated. Recognition is timely rather than premature.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism of the superconducting phase remains unsettled.
Relative weight of early independent experimental groups is not resolved by the supplied credit.
Whether the committee would consider the field still too young.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock, with the magic-wavelength idea enabling many atoms to be probed without Stark shift, brought fractional uncertainties to the 10^-18 level and opened precision tests of fundamental constants, relativistic redshift at millimetre scales and a redefinition of the second. A clear invention with lasting impact.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and first realised the strontium lattice clock; Ye developed it to the leading accuracy and stability. A two-person prize is clean, though other groups (e.g. ion and lattice clock teams) also contributed.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent clocks worldwide agree at extreme precision; this is mature and well confirmed, with the redefinition of the second pending.
uncertainties: Overlap with the earlier frequency comb and ion-clock recognitions could be seen as incremental by some members.
Credit to Pritchard-like earlier ideas on lattice spectroscopy is not covered in the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental observation of the Higgs boson with ATLAS and CMS completed the Standard Model and confirmed the mechanism recognised in 2013 for its theoretical prediction. This is the sort of decisive discovery that stands at the centre of the prize, and its importance is beyond doubt.
assessment.attribution: The discovery is a collaboration achievement of thousands; the supplied four names are founders/spokespeople and one must choose at most three. The choice of Gianotti, Jenni and Virdee is a defensible but contestable reading, and Della Negra is an equally strong founding figure for CMS. Prize rules make fair allocation difficult.
assessment.maturity: Fully confirmed by both experiments, with coupling measurements still improving; recognition is arguably overdue relative to the 2012 discovery.
uncertainties: Attribution to individuals within large collaborations is intrinsically contested.
Unclear whether the committee would recognise a collaboration-based discovery with this limit of three persons.
Which spokesperson or founder most fairly represents each experiment.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, together with the experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells, established a major new class of quantum matter and extended the topological ideas recognised in 2016.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele provided the theoretical foundation and Molenkamp's group the first experimental realisation (with theoretical proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang that is not in the credited names). The three-person set is natural but leaves out important contributors.
assessment.maturity: Many independent confirmations in multiple materials, including 3D topological insulators; the interpretation is stable and the field mature.
uncertainties: Omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and of experimental 3D topological insulator work, makes fair allocation delicate.
Partial overlap with the 2016 prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The detection of a diffuse flux of astrophysical high-energy neutrinos with IceCube opened neutrino astronomy and later identified a blazar and the Galactic plane as sources. A clear experimental discovery with broad astrophysical consequences.
assessment.attribution: Halzen was the driving force behind the IceCube concept and its realisation, while Karle played a major role in detector construction and analysis. The collaboration nature makes a two-person credit a simplification, and the supplied names omit other leaders.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse flux has been confirmed with independent analyses and source associations have emerged, though the origin of most of the flux remains unclear; timing is reasonable.
uncertainties: Source identification remains incomplete.
Credit across a large collaboration and the roles of early AMANDA colleagues.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Realising the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and later single-site resolved quantum gas microscopes created a new way to simulate strongly correlated many-body physics, with clear and lasting impact on condensed-matter and quantum information.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch) supplied the theoretical proposal, Bloch and Greiner the decisive early experiments and microscope. The configuration is coherent, but Jaksch and Hänsch-group contributions and parallel microscope groups are not in the credit list.
assessment.maturity: Extensively confirmed in many labs; the platform is mature, although the strongest scientific payoff (open problems such as high-Tc physics) is still pending.
uncertainties: Overlap with 2001 and 2012 cold-atom prizes.
Several candidates in this longlist share Bloch and Zoller, so the allocation across fields is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of high-temperature superconductivity in iron pnictides in 2008 created a second family of high-Tc superconductors and an entire field of unconventional superconductivity. A clean discovery, in the sense of the prize.
assessment.attribution: Hosono is credited as the sole discoverer, and his 2008 LaFeAsO paper triggered the field; rapid follow-on materials work (e.g. in China) was crucial but built on his discovery. A single-person award is defensible.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced and extended worldwide within weeks; the pairing mechanism is still unresolved, but the discovery itself is secure and about eighteen years old.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism unresolved.
Lower maximum Tc than cuprates may reduce perceived impact.
Possible competing contributions from early follow-up groups.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Horizon-scale imaging of M87* and Sgr A* provided direct visual evidence of a black-hole shadow and permitted new tests of strong-field gravity, which is of obvious interest to a gravity theorist. It is a clear observational discovery of lasting significance.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed the shadow imaging concept, Doeleman led the EHT VLBI effort, and Zensus built key European VLBI infrastructure; a three-person set is plausible but the collaboration is large and the decisive credit assignment is open.
assessment.maturity: Two independent targets have been imaged and polarisation results appear consistent, but the interpretation and test of GR remain model-dependent; the field is still young.
uncertainties: Model dependence of the parameter inferences.
Attribution among a large collaboration and early concept developers.
Possible prematurity compared with other candidates.
